metadata.title: When Short Loans Pay More: A Recession Warning
metadata.section: Section B: Macroeconomics, Money & Financial Conditions
metadata.visual_form: Bent line: one dot per loan length, green when normal, red when upside down
metadata.data_notes: The 30-year bond was paused 2002-2006; the 20-year yield fills that gap.

events.label: Curve inverts before the dot-com crash
COVID: short-term rates cut to near zero
Deepest inversion on the chart (-1.74 points)

explanation.summary: The interest rates the US government pays on loans from 3 months to 30 years. Normally longer loans pay more, so the line slopes up. When short-term rates rise above long-term rates, the curve is upside down ("inverted"). Inversions came before the recessions that began in 1990, 2001 and 2007. The deepest one, in 2023, has not been followed by a recession so far.
explanation.methodology: Treasury constant-maturity yields from FRED (DGS3MO, DGS6MO, DGS1, DGS2, DGS5, DGS10, DGS30), averaged by month. The US did not issue 30-year bonds from 2002 to 2006, so the 20-year yield fills that gap.

key_findings.title: 2000: Inversion Before the Dot-Com Bust
key_findings.description: The 3-month rate (5.94%) was above the 10-year rate (5.24%). A recession began in March 2001.
key_findings.significance: The inversion came about a year before the downturn.

key_findings.title: 2006: Inversion Before the Financial Crisis
key_findings.description: The 3-month rate (5.09%) was above the 10-year rate (4.88%). The Great Recession began in December 2007.
key_findings.significance: The warning came more than a year early.

key_findings.title: 2023: The Deepest Inversion on the Chart
key_findings.description: The 3-month rate (5.31%) was 1.74 points above the 10-year rate (3.57%). No recession followed so far. As of September 2026 the curve slopes up again (3-month 4.09%, 10-year 4.99%).
key_findings.significance: The most famous recession signal has not worked this time, at least not yet.
